newsitem.title: MALTA: Palestinian's Shaath says will meet Israel's Levy.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian's Shaath says will meet Israel's Levy.

text.p: Israeli and Palestinian ministers, after weeks of deadlock in the Middle East, will meet in Malta on the sidelines of a European-Mediterranean conference, a Palestinian minister said on Tuesday.
Planning Minister Nabil Shaath said he would meet Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, but no time had been fixed.

It will be the first time Israelis and Palestinians have met at this level since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered work to start on a Jewish settlement in disputed Arab East Jerusalem a month ago.
"There will be a meeting but not with (Palestinian President Yasser) Arafat," Shaath told Reuters. Asked if he himself would be meeting Levy, he said: "Yes."
The Europeans at the Malta conference have been pressing for an Israeli-Palestinian meeting in the hope of breaking the deadlock in Middle East peace talks.

But at the same time they are trying to stop the Middle East impasse wrecking their efforts to achieve progress on other aspects of relations between Europe and the Arabs, the largest bloc on the southern shores of the Mediterranean.

Delegates to the conference, which opened at 3.20 p.m. (1320 GMT) in what was once the hospital of the Knights of Malta, said disputes remain over how the foreign ministers should handle the Middle East conflict.

Twenty-seven delegations -- eight Arab delegates, the 15 European Union states plus Israel, Turkey, Cyprus and Malta -- are taking part in the conference, which aims to keep up the momentum of a dialogue started in Barcelona in 1995.
The delegates said the Arab states had tried to add a condemnation of Israeli settlement policies in the draft of the final statement but the Europeans wanted to keep this out.

"In the text on which we are working, we will want to recall the principles of the peace process. I don't think that we are seeking to go into the details of the (Middle East peace) negotiations," said French spokesman Yves Doutriaux.
Some Arab delegations have also floated the idea of making their own separate declaration on Middle East peace but the Europeans say they want to avoid this.

"Our wish is to find a formula on which there can be unanimity, to avoid unilateral declarations to which some are committed. The objective of the Barcelona process is to commit all the Euro-Mediterranean community," said Doutriaux.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo echoed the European view when he told the opening session that impasse on Middle East peace should not lead to impasse in the Barcelona process, which also addresses economic, social and cultural matters.
But in recognition of the gravity of the Middle East crisis, van Mierlo agreed to give double speaking time to Levy, Arafat and Algeria, coordinator of the Arab group.
Senior Arab officials met earlier on Tuesday and Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf said they wanted a reference to the Middle East stalemate in the final statement.

"I think when you try to assess the situation in the Mediterranean region and talk about political dialogue and security in this region you cannot avoid talking about the peace process in the Middle East because it is a major threat to the security and stability of the region," he told Reuters.
"We want the final declaration to make a reference to this situation and express a position regarding the stalemate the peace process is facing."

Other controversies, bracketed in a recent draft of the final statement, are over human rights, recognition of NGOs (non-governmental organisations) and the rights of emigrants -- mainly a reference to foreigners working in Europe.
